financial_summary: GREATLAND RES LTD. is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $3.8B market cap on $1.5B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +147% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +5.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 70% against a 10% cost of capital — a 60-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 63% confirm genuine pricing power.
The business throws off $521M in free cash flow — roughly 35 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Net dilution runs at 0.0% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 19% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 4.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 53% operating margin runs 43pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.03x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 222 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 49% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 4257% and a beta of 1.06, it moves roughly with the market.
Trading is thin (about $23K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 64% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 64% below its DCF fair value of $15.58, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $7.25 to $35.60 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 6.6 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 1.9 vs 7.9 and P/FCF 7.3 vs 21.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 13.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 31.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 6.3% annual cash-flow growth, 23pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 70% clears the cost of capital of 9.8% by 60pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
It runs a 63% gross margin and converts 35% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 39% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $842.5M.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
own: Insiders own 19.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 34%.
people: With about 560 employees, each generates about $2.7M of revenue, 4.3x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $930K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.8M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
